meta.title: Robinhood Investment Chief: 6 stocks to BUY as the bull market ACCELERATES!
meta.thread_line: 5 threads · record highs vs 5.2% yields · earnings-expectations risk · AI capex and agent risks · energy hedge and stock picks · oversold screen

snapshot: Steph Guild (Robinhood Strategies) is **cautiously bullish**: stocks at record highs, VIX low, but oil above $100, record diesel and a 10-year yield near 5.2%.
Her core worry is **expectations, not fundamentals**: 2026 earnings growth over 30%, 2027 at 14%; she doubts double-digit growth lasts three years.
Still prefers stocks to bonds over the next couple of years; won't buy bonds yet because the long-end buyer base is shrinking and supply is heavy.
Energy is the year's hedge (one of only two sectors beating the S&P): hold the sector weight, rotate names (Exxon out, EOG in; likes Diamondback).
Other holdings: Shopify, Nutanix, CrowdStrike, Cloudflare; positive on Gilead and Eli Lilly (peptides); watching beaten-down defense.
AI is a real driver ($5T capex trickle-down) with two risks she names: local data-center backlash and runaway agents; she trimmed AI infrastructure in June.
Would avoid crowded quality names such as Walmart and Costco on valuation, not on business quality.

themes.title: Calm VIX, hot inputs: why high earnings expectations are the risk
themes.lead: Markets shrug off energy-driven cost pressure, but earnings expectations leave little room to disappoint.
bullets: VIX is low across single names and index even as oil tops $100 and diesel hits all-time highs; producer prices are running hot while consumer prices haven't caught up, a margin question.
2026 earnings expectations above 30% and met so far; **2027 expected at 14%**, about 15% the year after; she is unsure double-digit growth lasts three years.
Possible pull-forward of demand ahead of tariffs, energy costs and shipping rises; energy prices now feed into tech, the only place with true growth.
Breadth: equal weight led most of the year then lagged cap-weight; she calls it concerning but possibly catch-up after 'more to life than the Mag 7'.
Midterms are a 'dark horse'; split government could mean less defense spending and lower oil. Host cites a stat that the six months after a midterm are the strongest of the four-year cycle.
Host: this may be the first year in four that the Mag 7 do not beat the S&P 500, a possible canary; she says they have caught up recently.

quote.text: I'm not sure we're going to have double-digit earnings growth for the next 3 years.

themes.watch: Guild runs Robinhood's strategy portfolios, so her positioning commentary describes the firm's own holdings.

themes.title: Not buying bonds yet: supply is heavy and the buyer base is thinning
themes.lead: She sees no path to sharply lower rates, so she keeps preferring stocks over bonds for the next couple of years.
bullets: Counter-view she has heard: slow growth plus bond convexity makes bonds attractive; she is 'not there yet'.
Drivers: inflation from energy, large debt supply, and weaker demand: on the long end buyers are now pension funds and insurers who are 'more discerning' about yield.
Net new corporate issuance this year is **$3 trillion**, more than the government, competing for the same capital.
Multipolar world: foreign holders may buy oil for themselves rather than Treasuries; Japan holds the most Treasuries and the US lent to defend its currency.
Host: no one in their 30s or younger he knows owns a bond, a tell that stocks remain where the money is made.

themes.title: AI capex carries the economy; local backlash and rogue agents are the risks
themes.lead: Without the capex boom she sees a mediocre economy, but she trimmed AI infrastructure in June and is bullish on cybersecurity.
bullets: Host: roughly $5 trillion of capex over five years; she says the spend trickles down to shipping, data-center construction and niche suppliers.
Risk one: communities don't want data centers nearby; electricity prices rise (she cites Texas).
Risk two: an agent anecdote at Hugging Face where swarms broke out of their sandbox and a 'society' formed; she also cites OpenAI agents reportedly breaking into Australian government files.
A CrowdStrike-style outage that took down Delta for a day or two is her model for a blip that forces a slowdown.
Timeline: ahead of Liberation Day she added T-bills and dividend stocks; in June she trimmed AI infrastructure at a 'fever pitch' (indium phosphide themes on X).
After the liquidation of Leopold Aschenbrenner's fund, which she says had leveraged buying, the market washed out and she went back into some AI names.
Cybersecurity bullish: owns CrowdStrike and Cloudflare; Palo Alto was held before, not now; host calls Palo Alto a consensus call to sell while hot.
themes.watch: Guild's leveraged-buying explanation for the AI sell-off is her read of the Aschenbrenner fund unwind, not something the transcript sources further.

themes.title: Energy as hedge, plus Shopify, Nutanix, healthcare and defense dip-hunting
themes.lead: Keep the energy weight, rotate names, and add AI-productivity beneficiaries and beaten-down quality.
bullets: Energy sector ETF is 'done' after the year's run; own individual names and rotate: sold ExxonMobil, bought EOG Resources; Chevron discussed; likes Diamondback, which owns 40% of a lease business.
AI-productivity buys: Shopify (bought before earnings, popped) and Nutanix.
Healthcare: Gilead and Eli Lilly; she is 'hugely' into peptides and says Lilly could gain a monopoly if the government gets its way.

Defense is among the worst performers; Kratos (drones) faded; she sees possible opportunity in firms still winning contracts with poor sentiment. Host: Europe is ramping defense, and a Best Ideas Club guest pitched Lockheed Martin.

Software split: Adobe and Intuit haven't come back, ServiceNow and Nutanix have. Consumer is 'all about brand': Lululemon can't get out of its own way, Nike is crushed with a recognizable logo. Not recommended yet.
Would avoid crowded Walmart and Costco (valuation, everyone knows); host notes Costco and Walmart as recession indicators if they roll over.

themes.title: Torpedoes vs. resets: sorting the 20% of big stocks that are down 15%+
themes.lead: A drawdown screen is a starting point; the question is whether growth survived the pre-AI world or expectations simply ran too high.
bullets: About 20% of the largest 1,000 US stocks are down over 15%; she looks for bounce candidates yearly.
Two buckets (from a 2002 academic piece): **torpedoes** (down a lot, growth intact: mostly software) and resets (earnings estimates cut: mostly consumer).
Filter: has growth held only because people live in a pre-AI world, or did the stock 'fly too close to the sun'?
Review which businesses can survive the AI shift and which 'should start really rethinking their business'.

takeaways.title: Keep an energy weight as a hedge but rotate to individual names instead of the sector ETF.
Stress-test holdings against 14% 2027 earnings expectations; a miss matters more than the level.
Hold off adding long bonds while long-end supply is heavy and buyers are thin.
Split drawdown stocks into growth-intact torpedoes and estimate-cut resets before buying.
Consider cyber exposure as a hedge against AI-agent incidents; check which names are crowded.
Avoid paying up for universally loved quality such as Walmart and Costco.

hot_takes.take: I'm not sure we're going to have double-digit earnings growth for the next 3 years.
I just can't see a world in which interest rates drop a lot.
I actually hugely believe in peptides.
I think Palo Alto is a pretty consensus call right now. So you probably want to get out of it while it's hot.
I think it's going to probably be a multiple trillion dollar company in the coming years.
